name: Fort Dearborn — commandant's quarters

grade.why: Pictured: a picture on the Images tab shows it.

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS THE FORT'S, NOT THIS BUILDING'S. No source reached dates any individual building inside Fort Dearborn. It opens with the rebuild of 1816 (Andreas; Wentworth quoting the Adjutant-General, 'the post was reoccupied about June, 1816 ... Nothing is on file respecting the rebuilding of the Fort') and closes with the demolition of the fort's principal structures in the summer of 1856 (Andreas). What carries the scene date is the middle: this building is drawn standing on the 1830 plan and described standing in Hubbard's 1827 walk round the inside, and the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

placement.position_note: READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN. Position in pixels on the plate Andreas reproduces at vol. 1 p. 113, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel (the scale derivation is on fort_dearborn_palisade and in docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md section 3), rotated to the sheet's true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221. Carry +/-20 percent on the offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself. The facade bearing is the fort's 8-degree rotation plus the side of the parade this building faces, because every range in this fort fronts the parade. Hubbard puts it exactly here in 1827: 'the brick building, just within the north stockade previously occupied by the commanding officers'. The 1830 plan draws a range against the north wall, west of the break in it, and that range is what this record measures.
placement.symbolic_location: Inside the north wall of Fort Dearborn, west of the north gate, fronting south onto the parade.

footprint.note: THE ONLY BUILDING IN THIS FORT WHOSE SIZE A SOURCE STATES. The key to Alexander Hesler's 1855 photograph, printed in Wentworth's 1881 address: 'the Commandant's Quarters, A (brick, about 25x50 ft.)'. 25 x 50 ft is 7.62 x 15.24 m, recorded converted with the original figures stated, per data/datum.json's units rule. IT IS ALSO THE CALIBRATION FOR EVERY OTHER DIMENSION IN THIS COMPLEX, which is worth stating plainly because it makes one number load-bearing far beyond its own building: the 1830 plan draws this range 48 pixels long, and setting 48 px = 50 ft is where the 1.10 ft/px scale comes from. The check that the calibration is not circular is the plate's own aspect - the drawn range is 1.9 times as long as it is deep against the key's stated 2.0 - and the parade width falling out at 71 ft against the same key's 80. THE DATE IS THE WEAKNESS: 'about 25x50' is a caption to a photograph taken twenty years after the scene date, and it is graded documented because it is a stated measurement of this building, not because 1855 is close to 1835.

kind.note: Hubbard 1827 has the commanding officers living in it; the 1855 key names it the Commandant's Quarters. Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort lists 'quarters for the officers' among what the stockade enclosed.

construction.note: Two independent statements twenty-eight years apart. Hubbard, 1827: 'the brick building, just within the north stockade'. The 1855 key: '(brick, about 25x50 ft.)'. THIS MATTERS BEYOND THIS BUILDING: docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 11 says there was 'no brick building of consequence yet on the south side' in 1835 and excepts the fort - correctly, and this is the building it means.

period_brick.note: T-3387: laid in K03's hand-made garrison brick (data/components/prairie_1904/k03_face_brick.json `soft_mud_red_garrison`): a soft, sand-struck, clamp-burnt red in wide lime joints, its colour the sheet's brick row (a shade darker), in the bonded K03 panel the 1904 walls wear, each brick shuffled. That this is brick is the record's construction and the archetype's stack argument; that it was a hand-made soft-mud brick of this colour and bond is the reconstruction (L-k03-period-brick-3387).

stories.note: Not stated. A 50 x 25 ft brick building housing the commanding officer of a two-company post, standing tall enough to be one of the 'two of the principal buildings of the Fort' identified in a photograph taken from across the river, is two storeys by type. The inference is from the building's size and its prominence, not from a statement.

wall_height_m.note: No height is attested for any building in this fort. 5.4 m is two storeys at about nine feet of interior height each plus floor structure, which is the ordinary figure for officers' quarters of this class. What is inferred is that the wall falls in this range, not that it is exactly 5.4 m.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for a rectangular range of this period, and it is what the building silhouetted in the 1855 photograph reads as. Inferred from type.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, and it is inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: The 1855 caption mentions the building's chimneys in passing while locating the ferry landing - 'under the west chimney of the Commandant's quarters' - which attests at least two by implying a west one and an east one. Two is the ordinary number for a double-pile range of this size in any case. WHERE they stood, how big they were and what they were made of are the archetype's, which is the standing admission in docs/LIBERTIES.md.

paint.note: Bare brick. Nothing says this building was rendered, painted or whitewashed; the whitewash in the sources belongs to the board fence of the 1850s compound and to John H. Kinzie's boyhood memory of the FIRST fort's blockhouses.

gallery.note: A PLAIN FRONT DOUBLE GALLERY, ADOPTED FOR JULY 1835 AS A BOUNDED CONTINUITY CHOICE (T-2388). The actual public-domain 1881 contained cut after Alexander Hesler’s 1855 photograph, with its explicit printed p.93 key, securely identifies this brick range as Commandant’s Quarters A and shows two gallery levels along its parade front. That strongest named picture governs the broad form; it does NOT date the gallery’s construction or prove it was unchanged in 1835. The existing interpretation identifies this with the brick commanding-officer range Hubbard describes inside the north stockade in 1827 and Harrison draws in 1830, under the fort’s 1816 rebuilding range. A front piazza is compatible with that retained fabric and arrangement; Hubbard’s distinct 1818 officers’ quarters already had an upper piazza, so the form is possible at this post before the scene date. That analogy supports plausibility, not identity or independent attestation of this gallery. We fairly choose continuity of the pictured plain gallery into 1 July 1835 rather than invent an alteration date. The occurrence IN THIS SCENE, every dimension, plain posts, deck, rails and canopy remain reconstructed. Existing full front width 15.24m, reach 2.1m, upper walk at the unchanged 2.7m storey line, 0.14m posts/deck and 0.95m rail are the existing gallery kit’s bounded choices. Footprint, surveyed placement, bearing188degrees, walls, roof, stacks and openings stay as before. No wraparound corner connection, additional stairs, unidentified 1850 soldiers’ gallery, paint or elaborate joinery is copied backwards.

gallery_storeys.note: Two levels follow the securely named 1855 A view: an open lower post level and an upper walk at the second floor. Carrying that arrangement into July1835 is the explicit reconstructed continuity choice in gallery, not an attested installation date. The existing5.4m wall and2.7m storey line stay fixed; exact deck, rail, pale rhythm, canopy fall and support sections remain liberties.

face_openings.note: The unchanged procedural layout written explicitly only so the existing gallery support solver clears every sash, casing and sill horn (T-2388). Captured directly from this range’s prior builder: four windows on each front storey, three on each rear storey, and one centred ground-floor front door; gable ends remain unread/empty as before. Every rectangle, sill, head, width and position is identical to the former default. Neither the 1855 picture nor an unkeyed earlier range is used to attest these counts or dimensions. The gallery’s original even support grid would intersect window trim; the existing explicit-opening API moves only its new supports onto solid piers.

function.note: Occupied by the commanding officer of the post; on 1835-07-01 that is Maj. John Greene, 5th Infantry (see fort_dearborn_palisade's occupants block). In 1827, with the post ungarrisoned, Dr. Alexander Wolcott the Indian Agent was living in it - which is Hubbard's reason for mentioning it at all.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS ONLY 16 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

residents.name: The commandant's household
residents.why: The commanding officer's quarters are a building in this dataset and he was the commanding officer. This is the one lives_at link in the parcel that is true by definition of the building rather than by evidence about the man. The record names a committed structure; the roof is the evidence's own limit and nothing narrower is claimed. COPIED FROM THE SINGULAR `lives_at` AND ITS RECONCILIATION ROW `hh_greene_john#lives_at`, changing no value, confidence or source. That field names the place as of 1 July 1835 and dates neither end of the relationship, so this row is `undated` rather than borrowing the scene date as a start (T-1273)

persons.name: Major John Greene
persons.note: THE MAN IN COMMAND ON THE SCENE DATE, on a tour that starts eighteen months before it and ends ten weeks after it. Three separately written accounts agree the fort was garrisoned through 1835, and the post surgeon's prescription book carries an entry dated 15 March 1835.

residents.research_note: THE FORT AS A HOUSEHOLD, WHICH IT WAS NOT - and the record says so rather than pretending. A garrison is not a family; it is a command with a strength, and this record names the one man the sources put at the head of it on 1 July 1835. THE ENLISTED MEN ARE DELIBERATELY NOT WRITTEN. data/structures/fort_dearborn_barracks.json records 'enlisted men of the 5th Infantry garrison' as its occupants and that is where they stay until a muster roll enters data/sources/. Inventing a company of privates would inflate the documented count with people no source names, which is precisely the error the grade vocabulary exists to make impossible.

citations.citation: Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, The Autobiography of Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard, Pa-pa-ma-ta-be, "The Swift Walker", with an Introduction by Caroline M. McIlvaine, Librarian of the Chicago Historical Society (Chicago: R. R. Donnelley & Sons Company, The Lakeside Press, Christmas 1911) — The Lakeside Classics. Read in full for its Chicago material before 1836: the front matter, McIlvaine's Introduction (pages ix-xxvii), and Hubbard's own narrative at pages 27-41, 135-138, 141-144, 153-159, 165-174 and 178-182. Hubbard's letter of 25 July 1827, printed as a note at page 174, is a separate source record.

transcribes.work: Hubbard's own autobiographical narrative — his engagement with the American Fur Company at Montreal and Mackinaw, the voyage of September 1818, his first entry into Chicago on 1 October 1818, the fort and its neighbours as he first saw them, the Chicago portage and Mud Lake, Hubbard's Trail, the trading posts of the Illinois River, and the Winnebago Scare of 1827 — ending abruptly at November 1830
transcribes.date: Written in the 1880s; printed 1888 and again 1911. Describes 1818-1830.
transcribes.note: A participant's recollection at more than fifty years' distance, and the rung most of this reading sits on. It is a recollection and not a record: the Fort Dearborn measurements are paces remembered, the payment of page 167 is dated to the wrong year, and the commanders' list is Hubbard's own search of the War Department records, which he says failed for the years after June 1833. The Winnebago Scare section (pages 166-174) is footnoted as coming not from the Diary but 'from statements by Mr. Hubbard in Chicago Historical Series, No. 10', which is one remove further.

transcribes.work: Caroline M. McIlvaine's Introduction, pages ix-xxvii — a 1911 review of the fifty-six years the Autobiography does not cover, compiled from letters, memoranda, contemporaries' reminiscences and printed history, and quoting E. O. Gale's Reminiscences of Early Chicago, The Chicago American of 10 October 1835, the Sunday Times of 24 October 1875 and Henry E. Hamilton's 1907 biographical sketch
transcribes.note: EVERY STATEMENT THIS PROJECT TAKES ABOUT 1834, 1835 OR 1836 COMES FROM HERE AND NOT FROM HUBBARD. The brick building at La Salle and South Water, the five or six hundred inhabitants, the brig Illinois of 25 May 1835, the Green Tree Tavern, the fire engine, the Russell & Mather purchase, the canal commissioners and the water-works are all McIlvaine's, written seventy-six years after the scene, and several are quotations at a further remove. A run reaching for 'Hubbard on 1835' is reaching for McIlvaine.

transcribes.work: Editorial notes by Henry E. Hamilton, signed H. E. H., inserted in square brackets in the narrative — including the note at page 178 that the hog-driving of 1829-30 'was the beginning of the packing industry in Chicago' — and the publishers' preface and closing note
transcribes.date: 1888 (the notes); 1911 (the preface and the closing note, the latter signed C. M. M.)
transcribes.note: Compiler's judgements, sixty years after the events, printed inside the narrative's own type. bk_hub_101 and bk_hub_104 are read from this layer and say so.

what_it_supplies: Fort Dearborn's occupation chronology, dated to the day, from its establishment in 1804 to its final abandonment on 29 December 1836 — which puts the scene year inside a continuous garrison running from 1 October 1832

a full description of the second fort as a man who lived beside it in 1818 remembered it: fourteen-foot oak pickets, a block house at the south-west corner and a bastion at the north-west, whitewashed stockade and buildings, the officers' quarters outside the pickets with a piazza at second-storey level, the soldiers' quarters, the sutler's store in the north-east corner, two gates, two ten-foot guardhouses, a two-storey commissary storehouse and a brick magazine

the fort's surroundings: a four-acre garden, a military barn, a field running half a mile south, the ONE road, a fence line closed from river to river, the well by the south gate, and wash-houses on the sandy beach east of the pickets

the Factor House — two storeys, squared logs, a split-picket fence, Jouett to about 1810 and then John Dean — and the American Fur Company's round-log storehouse built by John Craft and occupied after his death by Jean Baptiste Beaubien

John Kinzie's house described from inside it: a long log cabin with a rude piazza, fronting the river directly opposite the fort, with a window that had a sight-line to the fort at night — the piazza confirmed again nine years later

a complete building count for the whole of the present Cook County in 1818: the fort's group, the Factor House, the Fur Company storehouse, Hardscrabble, Ouilmette's cabin and Kinzie's house, and nothing else

the river mouth's history — its natural outlet at the fort, its southward migration behind a sand spit driven by north-east winds, its position at The Pines a mile south as late as 1827, the soldiers' cut of spring 1828 and the sand's refilling of it

landscape: the prairie seen from Douglas Grove, the Blue Island grove and the Desplaines timber, wild onion and leek along the river, wild rice and head-high grass at Mud Lake, the old cultivated field on the River Guarie still legible as cornhills, and prairie fires dangerous enough to sink boats against

Hubbard's Trail, dated by the man who cut it (1822 to Danville, extended north to Chicago in 1824) and the State road from Vincennes to Chicago ordered in the winter of 1833-34 that adopted most of it
the settlement's size taken sideways: about forty men and women turned out to fight the fort fire in 1827, and a majority of the men at the fort that summer were Hubbard's own employees

for 1835, at one remove through McIlvaine: the brig Illinois lightered ashore on 25 May because the harbour could not take her, the passengers going on to the Green Tree Tavern, the Chicago American of 10 October 1835 on Hubbard's fire engine, and the March 1835 purchase of the eighty acres of Russell & Mather's addition for $5,000
one period document, and it is graded separately: Hubbard's letter to his sister headed 'Chicago, July 25, 1827', at data/sources/hubbard_letter_1827_07_25.json
what_it_does_not_supply: Hubbard's own eyewitness on 1835. HIS NARRATIVE ENDS IN NOVEMBER 1830 and the closing note says so in as many words; the book's 1835 is Caroline McIlvaine's, written in 1911

any plat position, lot, or measured coordinate. Every placement here is prose — 'west and a little south of the fort', 'about where Wells street now crosses the river' — and several are given in streets that did not exist when the thing described did
reliable dimensions. 'A square of about six hundred feet' for the Fort Dearborn stockade is a pace-estimate at sixty years' distance and is much larger than the fort this project reconstructs

a consistent account of the officers' quarters: page 36 puts them outside the pickets and built of hewn logs, page 167 puts the commanding officers' former quarters in a brick building just within the north stockade and the log quarters within the pickets on the west. The book contradicts itself and this project does not resolve it
the right year for the Pottawatomie payment and the fort fire: page 167 prints 1828 where the section heading, the surrounding narrative and Hubbard's own dated letter all say July 1827
the names of the officers commanding Fort Dearborn after 19 June 1833 — Hubbard says he could not find them in the War Department records, so the source names nobody in command during the scene year
a residence for anybody in 1835. Every person Hubbard names, he names for what they did between 1812 and 1830

research_note: THE ONE BUILDING IN FORT DEARBORN WITH A STATED SIZE, and therefore the building the whole complex is measured against. Its footprint note explains why that is both the strength of this record and a risk running through every other record in the fort. Two guards. The '25 x 50 ft' is a caption to an 1855 photograph, not a survey. And the 1855 key's phrase 'occupying the north-west corner of the enclosure' covers this building and the officers' quarters together as a pair seen from across the river; it is not a statement that this range stood in the corner, and Hubbard puts it 'just within the north stockade', which is where the 1830 plan draws it. See docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md. T-2388 now adopts the securely identified 1855 A front double gallery as an explicit RECONSTRUCTED continuity choice for July1835, with no invented construction/alteration date. The older plan/Hubbard range identity and placement control; the new gallery does not identify or copy an unknown soldiers’ range.
